answer.exemplar: Blake printed each poem and its plate on the two faces of one sheet, coloured the plates by hand and had copies interleaved so that text faced image. About a dozen copies survive, each differently coloured and sometimes differently worded, so no single authoritative text exists and editors must collate the copies against each other.

questions.explanation: Because each copy was coloured by hand and bound in interleaved sheets, the work exists as a family of objects. The differences between copies are differences in wording as well as in colour.
questions.hint: Think of printed sheets, hand colour and interleaving.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Ottava rima distinguished from the Spenserian stanza
questions.learningObjective: Explain how ottava rima differs from the Spenserian stanza and name a poem in each.
questions.stem: Your notes set down an eight-line stanza beside a nine-line one. Explain how ottava rima differs from the Spenserian stanza, and name a later Romantic poem that uses each form.

answer.exemplar: Ottava rima is an eight-line stanza of iambic pentameter rhyming ABABABCC, inherited from Chaucer through Boccaccio and used by Shelley in Adonais. The Spenserian stanza has nine lines, ABABBCBCC, with a final alexandrine, and was used by Byron in Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.

questions.explanation: Both forms are rhymed pentameter, so line count and rhyme pattern are the only reliable discriminators. The Spenserian stanza interlocks its rhymes across the quatrain.
questions.hint: Count lines and look for the long closing foot.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The account of composition given in the Lyrical Ballads preface
questions.learningObjective: Explain the preface's claim about the poet's office and the making of a poem.
questions.stem: You copy the sentence about legislation out of the preface to Lyrical Ballads and find it hard to place. Explain what the preface claims about the poet's office, and what it claims a poem is made of.

answer.exemplar: The preface claims that poets are the unacknowledged legislators of the world, meaning that their shaping of language and feeling guides a nation without formal office or public credit. It defines a poem as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings, taking its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity, which is why the book treats ordinary rural life and common speech as worthy subjects.

questions.explanation: The two claims work together: a poem begins in private recollection and becomes public in effect. Treating either claim alone makes the preface sound narrower than it is.
questions.hint: Set the legislator phrase beside the definition of a poem.

answer.exemplar: The couplet stands after every second quatrain and turns description into judgement, generalising from the particular graves and ploughmen of the churchyard to a maxim about mortality and hidden worth. questions.topic: The marginal prose gloss in The Rime of the Ancient Mariner
questions.learningObjective: Explain the glosses' function and the effect of their removal from later printings.
questions.stem: You wonder why the marginal glosses of the 1817 sea narrative were not repeated in later printings. Explain what they do and why their disappearance changes how the poem is read.

questions.hint: Hold constant everything except the edition.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Ottava rima distinguished from the Spenserian stanza
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difference between the two forms and the effect of the extra line.
questions.stem: You need to explain to a club why a ninth line of twelve feet changes the character of a stanza. Explain the difference between the two forms and the effect of the extra line.

answer.exemplar: An ottava rima stanza runs to eight lines of iambic pentameter closed by a rhyming couplet, so its rhymes arrive in pairs and its movement is quick. The Spenserian stanza interlocks its rhymes across the quatrain and adds a ninth line in alexandrine, and that long closing line slows the stanza right down, giving the close a weight that the quicker form never has.

questions.explanation: The difference is structural: eight lines with a couplet against nine with an interlocking chain and a long close. The extra foot at the end produces weight and finality rather than speed.
questions.hint: Ask whether the extra foot arrives early or late.

questions.explanation: The prose notice mattered more, because it framed the poem as a fragment by an unknown writer and set the terms of reception. Ranking the title page first avoids the comparison the question asks for.

questions.topic: The couplet every two quatrains in Gray's Elegy
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the work of the couplets from the work of the quatrains.
questions.stem: You ask what the couplets of Gray's Elegy contribute that the quatrains do not. Which statement is best?

options.text: They generalise, turning the particular scene just described into a statement about all human life.
They describe, giving the physical detail that the quatrains leave out.
options.misconception: assigns the couplets the quatrains' descriptive work

options.text: They narrate, advancing the story of the speaker's life to its conclusion.
options.misconception: makes the couplets carry the plot

options.text: They confess, stating the poet's private doubts about his own calling.
options.misconception: makes the couplets an autobiographical confession

questions.explanation: The quatrains render particular graves, labours and dwellings. Description, narration and private confession are the work of other parts of the poem.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Blake's Songs as a set of hand-coloured copies rather than an edition
questions.learningObjective: Defend the claim that the colouring of the songbook is part of its making.
questions.stem: You argue that the illuminated songbook's colouring is not decoration but argument. What grounds support you?

options.text: Its pages are printed on both sides, so the pictures must be essential to the sense.
options.misconception: rests the argument on the page layout alone

options.text: Its copies are coloured by different hands, so the colouring is part of the making, not a later finish.
Its plates show the same scene repeatedly, so the images carry the sequence of the songs.
options.misconception: claims the plates repeat a single scene

options.text: Its sheets are interleaved, so no reader could see the pictures at all.
options.misconception: ignores the way interleaving works

questions.explanation: If each copy is coloured by a different hand, then colouring belongs to the production of the work. Page layout and interleaving are real features, but they do not make the colour an argument.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The 1800 second state of Lyrical Ballads and its added prefaces
questions.learningObjective: Draw the full set of conclusions supported by the 1800 volume's catalogue entry.

stimulus.body: A catalogue entry for a volume of lyrical ballads records a printed date of 1800, a publisher's name, a new prefatory essay, two poems that do not appear in the 1798 volume, and a second group of poems placed at the end rather than the beginning. It also notes that the sheets of the earlier printing appear at the back.

questions.stem: Which set of conclusions about the 1800 volume does the catalogue entry support?

options.text: The 1800 volume reprinted the 1798 text with only a new binding and no other change.
options.misconception: assumes nothing but the binding changed

options.text: The 1800 volume was a reprint made after the poet's death, so it cannot be his own edition.
options.misconception: dates the volume after the poet's death

options.text: The 1800 volume reversed the order, added a preface and two poems, and was bound with leftover 1798 sheets.
The 1800 volume dropped the poems that had appeared in the 1798 volume altogether.
options.misconception: assumes the earlier poems were dropped

questions.explanation: Each element of the entry matches a known change in 1800: a new essay, two added poems, a reordered collection, and leftover 1798 sheets. The alternatives contradict the entry itself.
questions.hint: Match each detail of the entry to a change in the volume.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The account of composition given in the Lyrical Ballads preface
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the preface redefines what poetry may treat as its subject.
questions.stem: In your seminar you set out to explain how the preface to the lyrical ballads turns a reader's idea of what may be written about. Explain the argument it makes.

answer.exemplar: The preface argues that the best poetry grows from the incidents and situations of common life and from the language men and women actually use, rather than from an artificial diction. It defines a poem as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings, taking its origin from emotion recollected in tranquillity, and it claims for poets the office of unacknowledged legislators, so that rural labours, cottages and children become proper material for verse.

questions.explanation: The preface's argument is about subject matter and language together: if feeling recollected in tranquillity is the source of a poem. That is why the volume can defend rural material without apology.
questions.hint: Ask what the preface says poetry is made from.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The account of a moment of composition told to another poet
questions.learningObjective: Compare two kinds of composition as the printed confession presents them.
questions.stem: You compare two moments of composition: one carefully planned over months, one arriving whole in a sleep and then being lost. Which does the printed confession treat as more valuable, and why?

options.text: The planned composition, because a poem that lasts months will be better made.
options.misconception: judges the two by length of labour alone

options.text: Neither, since the poet claims that no poem can be valued at all.
options.misconception: turns the confession into a denial of all value

options.text: Both equally, since the poet only wanted to explain his working method.
options.misconception: reads the confession as a neutral methods note

options.text: The interrupted sleep, because what it gave was unrepeatable, and the loss is part of what the poem records.

questions.explanation: The confession is an argument for the accidental, unrepeatable gift. Treating the two compositions as equal, or valuing the labour, inverts the preference the printed account makes.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two could not have been extended.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Ottava rima distinguished from the Spenserian stanza
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the expressive effect of a stanza whose rhymes come in pairs.
questions.stem: You ask why a later poet chose a form whose rhymes come in pairs rather than a form whose rhymes interlock. What effect does the choice of the paired form have?

options.text: The pairing makes the stanza heavy and slow, so the poem turns back upon itself.
options.misconception: claims the paired rhymes slow the stanza down

options.text: The pairing gives the stanza a quick, regular pulse, which suits the poem's onward and biographical movement.
The pairing removes the need for rhyme, so the poem becomes a free verse text.
options.misconception: confuses a rhyme scheme with the absence of rhyme

options.text: The pairing is a technical convenience that carries no expressive weight.
options.misconception: denies the form any expressive function

questions.explanation: Rhymes in pairs settle quickly and keep the stanza moving. The interlocking form slows things down instead, and neither choice makes rhyme disappear or carry no expressive weight.
questions.hint: Listen to the closing pair: does it hurry or halt?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The title-page wording of Gray's Elegy across its early editions
questions.learningObjective: Assess the effect of the printed notice on the poem's reception.

stimulus.body: A printed notice stands at the head of a new edition of a poem and speaks of a poem written in a country churchyard by a person of no great name, and hints that what the reader holds is only a part of a larger design that was never carried out.

questions.stem: Judging from the printed notice, what does it do to the way the poem is received?

options.text: It announces that the poem is a complete work of the highest achievement.
options.misconception: reads the notice as praise of the poem's completeness

options.text: It explains the poem's metre so that readers can scan it correctly.
options.misconception: treats the notice as a technical explanation of metre

options.text: It presents the poem as a fragment by an unknown writer, lowering its status before the reader has begun.
It names the subscribers who paid for the printing of the edition.
options.misconception: imagines the notice to be a list of subscribers

questions.explanation: By crediting the work to nobody and calling it an unfinished part. That framing is what makes the notice matter, rather than anything it says about metre or subscribers.
questions.hint: Read the notice's claim about the writer and completeness.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: The couplet every two quatrains in Gray's Elegy
questions.learningObjective: Describe the stanza of Gray's Elegy and its structural contribution.
questions.stem: In a lecture on period verse you set out to describe the stanza of Gray's Elegy. Explain the pattern of the quatrains and the couplets, and what the pattern contributes.

answer.exemplar: The poem is written in quatrains of iambic tetrameter rhyming alternately, and after every second quatrain comes a rhyming couplet in the same four-foot measure, with a final couplet closing the whole poem. The regular return of the couplet acts as a pulse, gathering the poem's meditation of humble graves and hidden worth into a series of settled statements, so the elegy arrives at its conclusions by steps rather than by a single rush.

questions.explanation: Describing the metre is only half the account; the pattern also organises the poem's thinking. A lecture that lists the units without explaining the alternation has described the shape.
questions.hint: Give the metre and then say what the arrangement does.

questions.learningObjective: Defend the claim that the illuminated songbook has no authoritative text.
questions.stem: You must defend the claim that the illuminated songbook has no authoritative text. Which set of reasons is strongest?

options.text: The songbook was never printed at all, so no question of an authoritative text arises.
options.misconception: denies that the work was printed

options.text: The songbook's text was destroyed by fire, and only the pictures survive.
options.misconception: invents a destruction of the printed sheets

options.text: The publisher chose one copy at random and forbade the others from being read.
options.misconception: imagines a publisher enforcing a single copy

questions.explanation: The claim rests on facts about the making: hand colouring. The alternatives invent a non-existent destruction, a prohibition, or an unprinted work, none of which the copies themselves support.
questions.hint: Ground the claim in how the copies were made.
